title: Biophysical Clustering of Single-Cell Data
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter examines the biophysical foundations of cell clustering and classification from single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq). It reviews why standard low-dimensional heuristic embeddings distort biological variation, introduces mechanistic clustering via the `meK-Means` framework, and shows how causal models of nascent (unspliced) and mature (spliced) RNA joint distributions define cell types directly through transcription parameters. ## Pitfalls of Low-Dimensional Embeddings The standard workflow in single-cell transcriptomics compresses high-dimensional molecular count matrices into two-dimensional visualizations using non-linear dimensional reduction algorithms such as t-SNE or UMAP, followed by distance-based graph clustering (e.g., Louvain or Leiden community detection). As shown by Chari and Pachter (2023), these low-dimensional embeddings can be profoundly specious. Dimensional reduction procedures warp metric distances, break global topologies, and frequently project arbitrary geometric configurations that do not reflect genuine biophysical relationships or true phenotypic separations. Distances between clusters in embedding spaces do not correspond to continuous physical coordinates, and the resulting cluster boundaries are highly sensitive to algorithmic hyperparameters rather than cellular mechanisms. When multimodal datasets are introduced—such as the simultaneous measurement of unspliced pre-mRNA ($u$) and spliced mature mRNA ($s$)—standard pipelines treat modalities independently or perform heuristic multimodal integration. This ignores the causal physical pathway linking transcription, splicing, and degradation, treating correlated counts as abstract coordinates rather than the outcome of an underlying kinetic process. ## Mechanistic Cell Type Inference: meK-Means To resolve the ambiguities of heuristic clustering, Chari, Gorin, and Pachter (2023) introduced **meK-Means** (mechanistic $K$-Means). Instead of minimizing Euclidean distances in an abstract latent space, meK-Means defines a cell cluster by a shared set of biophysical kinetic rates. ### The Underlying Chemical Master Equation Single-cell sequencing protocols using unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) output integer count matrices. The generation of unspliced counts $u$ and spliced counts $s$ within a single cell can be modeled via the Chemical Master Equation (CME) describing the telegraph or bursty model of transcription coupled with downstream RNA processing: $$\text{Gene Switch:} \quad G_{\text{off}} \xrightleftharpoons[k_{\text{off}}]{k_{\text{on}}} G_{\text{on}}$$ $$\text{Synthesis:} \quad G_{\text{on}} \xrightarrow{k_r} G_{\text{on}} + U$$ $$\text{Processing (Splicing):} \quad U \xrightarrow{\beta} S$$ $$\text{Degradation:} \quad S \xrightarrow{\gamma} \emptyset$$ Here, $U$ denotes unspliced pre-mRNA and $S$ denotes mature spliced mRNA. In bursty regimes where the promoter activation rate is small relative to deactivation ($k_{\text{off}} \gg k_{\text{on}}$), transcription occurs in bursts of average size $b = k_r / k_{\text{off}}$ occurring at frequency $k_{\text{on}}$. Let $\boldsymbol{\theta}_g = (k_{\text{on}}, k_{\text{off}}, k_r, \beta, \gamma)_g$ represent the kinetic parameters for gene $g$. The CME defines the theoretical stationary joint probability distribution $P(u, s \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}_g)$. ### Measurement Models and Technical Noise Raw single-cell sequencing does not capture every transcript. Given an experimental capture efficiency $p_{\text{cap}}$, the probability of observing $m$ unspliced and $n$ spliced molecules given true counts $u$ and $s$ is modeled as a binomial sampling process: $$P(m, n \mid u, s) = \binom{u}{m} p_{\text{cap}}^m (1 - p_{\text{cap}})^{u - m} \binom{s}{n} p_{\text{cap}}^n (1 - p_{\text{cap}})^{s - n}$$ The observable joint probability $P(m, n \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}_g)$ convolves the biophysical distribution with this technical noise model. ### The meK-Means Formulation In meK-Means, a cluster $k \in \{1, \dots, K\}$ is characterized by a parameter matrix $\boldsymbol{\Theta}^{(k)} = \{\boldsymbol{\theta}_1^{(k)}, \dots, \boldsymbol{\theta}_G^{(k)}\}$ across all genes $G$. For a single cell $i$ with observed count profile $\mathbf{X}_i = \{(m_{ig}, n_{ig})\}_{g=1}^G$, the algorithm assigns the cell to the cluster that maximizes the joint biophysical likelihood: $$k_i^* = \arg\max_k \sum_{g=1}^G \log P\left(m_{ig}, n_{ig} \;\middle|\; \boldsymbol{\theta}_g^{(k)}\right)$$ The algorithm iterates between two core steps until convergence: 1. **Assignment step:** Assign each cell $i$ to its optimal cluster $k_i^*$ using the current kinetic parameter sets $\boldsymbol{\Theta}^{(k)}$. 2. **Update step:** Given cell assignments $\{i : k_i^* = k\}$, re-estimate the parameter vectors $\boldsymbol{\Theta}^{(k)}$ across the cells assigned to each cluster by maximum likelihood or method of moments over the bivariate CME solution. By formulating clustering around the parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ of the CME, meK-Means replaces heuristic geometric proximities with biophysically interpretable invariants: cells belong to the same cluster if and only if their RNA profiles are generated by the same kinetic regime of transcription, splicing, and degradation. ## Alternative Biophysical Paradigms: biVI and Chronocell While meK-Means operates by partitioning cells into discrete steady-state kinetic clusters, related biophysical inference tools handle orthogonal biological settings: * **biVI (Biophysical Variational Inference):** When discrete clusters do not capture continuous cell-to-cell variability, `biVI` pairs bivariate CME steady-state models with variational autoencoders. Rather than computing fixed discrete kinetic clusters $\boldsymbol{\Theta}^{(k)}$, `biVI` learns a continuous low-dimensional latent space that maps directly to individual single-cell biophysical parameters. * **Chronocell:** In systems where cell populations exist along continuous developmental trajectories rather than at steady state, standard static clustering breaks down. `Chronocell` reformulates the problem from descriptive pseudotime to physical *process time*. It uses the time-dependent, non-steady-state CME to track the dynamic transitions between states, providing an identifiable model that bridges continuous trajectories and discrete kinetic clustering. ## Sources * `NOTES: Contributions clustering`: References to Chari and Pachter (2023) on distortions in low-dimensional embeddings, and Chari, Gorin, and Pachter (2023) on meK-Means formulation. * `NOTES: meK-means: Biophysically interpretable inference of cell types`: Abstract and operational details of the meK-Means algorithm and `monod.mminference`. * `NOTES: Pachter Lab Biophysics Home` & `NOTES: Packages`: Comparison table of tools (`Monod`, `biVI`, `meK-Means`, `Chronocell`) outlining modality assumptions, technical noise modeling, and resolution. * `NOTES: biVI: Biophysical modeling with variational autoencoders`: Context on variational autoencoder integration of bivariate CME models. * `NOTES: Chronocell: Trajectory inference from single-cell data`: Contrast between discrete clustering and continuous process-time trajectory inference. * `NOTES: Theory and Computation of Transcriptional Dynamics`: Background on CME solutions, binomial capture models (Tang et al.), and kinetic models of splicing.
